steps.title: Who said what?
paragraphs: “Did you take my headphones?” “No, I didn’t.” “Then why are they in your bag?” “I don’t know!” “Mom!”
Read it again. How many people are talking? Who shouted “Mom!”?
Without tags and new lines, a conversation turns into a puzzle. Writers use two tools to fix that: speech tags, and a new line every time the speaker changes.

cards.title: Three places for the tag
cards.body: Before: Leo said, “I’m starving.” After: “I’m starving,” Leo said. In the middle (a split quote): “I’m starving,” said Leo, “so let’s eat.” Moving the tag keeps a conversation from sounding the same every time.

cards.title: Split quotes
cards.text:
One sentence, split: “If we hurry,” said Mia, “we can catch the bus.”
Two sentences: “We missed the bus,” said Mia. “Let’s walk.”
cards.note: If the quote is one sentence, put a comma after the tag and carry on with a small letter. If a new sentence starts, put a full stop after the tag and start with a capital.

cards.title: New speaker, new line
cards.body: Start a new paragraph (a new line, indented) every time a different person speaks. Then readers can follow a conversation even when you leave some tags out.

cards.title: Tags that tell more
cards.body: “Said” is fine most of the time: readers hardly notice it. Now and then, a stronger tag (whispered, snapped, muttered, called) or an action (Leo grabbed his bag.) shows how the words were spoken.

prompts: Which line in your conversation has the best tag or action? Why does it work?
How did starting a new line for each speaker change how easy your scene is to read?
